cards.back: A defined region in space across whose boundary mass, energy, and momentum may flow.
A condition where stored quantities do not change with time, though through-flows can persist.
Diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, J=−D∇C.
A dimensionless comparison of reaction and transport timescales; convention depends on the process being modeled.
Dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous effects, Re=ρUL/μ.
The ideal laminar pressure-driven flow of a Newtonian fluid through a straight circular tube.
A material coefficient relating conductive heat flux to temperature gradient.
Temperature drop per heat-transfer rate for a specified geometry and boundary model.
For a one-sided slab with zero-order uptake, L_c = √(2 D C₀ / q); beyond it the core is oxygen-depleted in the model.
Doubling surface oxygen raises the critical thickness by √2, not 2, so supplying more oxygen has diminishing returns.
φ² = q L² / (D C₀) compares diffusion time L²/D with the depletion time C₀/q; values of order 1 or more mean the interior is depleted.
A negative predicted concentration means a depleted region where the zero-order assumption fails; use a saturating uptake law.
Steady heater: Q̇ = ṁ c_p (T_out − T_in) with ṁ = ρQ.
Re = ρvD/μ; tube flow laminar below about 2,000.
ΔP = 128μLQ/(πD⁴): halving D raises ΔP sixteenfold.
τ_w = 32μQ/(πD³) in laminar tube flow; cells respond to shear.
τ ≈ L²/D: 5 s for 100 μm, 500 s for 1 mm and 3.5 h for 5 mm at D = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s; ten times the distance takes a hundred times as long.
C(x, t) = C₀ erfc(x/(2√(Dt))) for a semi-infinite medium with constant surface concentration; the front moves as √t.
erfc(η) = 0.5 at η = 0.477, so t₅₀ ≈ 1.1 x²/D; the 1% front is at 3.64 √(Dt).
Valid until the profile reaches the far side (t ≲ L²/(16 D)); needs a constant surface concentration, constant D and no reaction.
Pe = UL/D = t_diff/t_adv; much larger than 1 means advection controls along that length; it depends on the length chosen.
N = k_c (C_bulk − C_wall); Sh = k_c d/D, which is 3.66 for fully developed laminar tube flow with a uniform wall concentration.
In fully developed laminar flow, k_c does not depend on flow rate; faster flow helps by replenishing the bulk along the tube, not by changing the transfer across it.
Sc = ν/D is of order 10² to 10³ in liquids; the concentration boundary layer is thinner than the velocity one by about Sc^(−1/3).
R_c = √(6DC₀/q) (centre just reaches zero): 346 μm for D = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, C₀ = 0.2 and q = 0.02, against 200 μm for the slab.
For R > R_c, C(r) = (q/6D)(r² − 3 r_n² + 2 r_n³/r) outside a core of radius r_n; r_n solves C₀ = (q/6D)(R² − 3 r_n² + 2 r_n³/R).
A 400 μm sphere has a core of 130 μm (3.5% of the volume); at 500 μm the core is 257 μm (13.5%); the rim is not a constant thickness.
t = 3 t_d log₂(R_c/R₀) for volume doubling every t_d; R_c grows as √C₀ and as 1/√q.
v = V_max C/(K_m + C): half of V_max at C = K_m, 90% at 9 K_m, first order with rate constant V_max/K_m at low C.
Using V_max at every concentration overestimates the uptake where C is comparable with K_m (a factor of 1.25 at C = 0.02 for K_m = 0.005).
With saturable uptake the minimum in a slab approaches zero gradually: 0.023 mol/m³ at the zero-order critical thickness of 200 μm and 0.002 at 250 μm in the synthetic example.
Define the limit by a functional threshold; function is lost at oxygen levels well above K_m, so the zero-order critical thickness is a first estimate, not the edge of function.
T(t) = T_∞ + (T₀ − T_∞) e^(−t/τ), τ = ρ c_p V/(h A); for a sphere V/A = D/6; time to a target = τ ln((T₀ − T_∞)/(T − T_∞)).
Bi = h (V/A)/k compares internal conduction with surface convection; the lumped model needs Bi well below about 0.1.
Conduction takes about R²/α (the slowest decay R²/(π² α) for a sphere); if it exceeds the external time constant, the interior controls and a higher h does not help proportionally.
After one time constant only 63% of the change has occurred; the exponential approach never completes in finite time.
τ = V/Q; wash-in C/C_in = 1 − e^(−t/τ) (95% at 3 τ); washout C/C₀ = e^(−t/τ) (1% at 4.6 τ).
With first-order uptake k, C_ss/C_in = 1/(1 + kτ) and the effective time constant is τ/(1 + kτ); kτ compares residence and consumption times.
N equal tanks have the same mean residence time but a sharper response, 1 − e^(−Nx) Σ (Nx)^k/k!; the relative SD of the residence time is 1/√N, and large N approaches plug flow.
Dead volume, bypass and long thin channels make the real response differ from the perfect-mixing result; a tracer experiment measures it.
Count the replicate profiles and average the oxygen readings at each depth; the construct is the replicate.
C_end = C₀ − qL²/(2D) at the sealed face of a one-sided slab; solve for q with L in metres.
L_c = √(2DC₀/q); a slab thicker than L_c has an anoxic zone of thickness L − L_c, and the profile above it does not depend on the thickness.
Zero-order uptake is an idealization: real uptake saturates, so the edge of the anoxic zone is softer, and oxygen above zero does not prove viability.
ΔC_r = (q/(4D))[2R_t² ln(R_t/r_c) − (R_t² − r_c²)] from the channel to the edge of the Krogh cylinder; it falls rapidly with the channel spacing.
ΔC_ax = π(R_t² − r_c²) ℓ q / Q: the oxygen used along the channel divided by the flow; more flow reduces it but not the radial drop.
At the outlet end at the tissue edge: C_in − ΔC_ax − ΔC_r; an adequate inlet value does not guarantee supply.
Closer channels reduce both drops; test the model with oxygen at the tissue edge at several axial positions on independent constructs.
